tytul: Whey ricotta with vinegar (UCCE recipe after NMSU)
wstep: This card follows the UCCE whey ricotta recipe, adapted from NMSU Extension: whole milk is added to fresh whey, heated to 185 °F (85 °C), and vinegar is added slowly.

akapity: Use whey and milk only from pasteurized milk; raw milk must be pasteurized before it is used for cheese.
Start heating the whey as soon as it has been separated from the curd.
The recipe heats the whey to 185 °F (85 °C) and uses vinegar of 5% acidity; it gives no amount of lemon juice, so do not replace the vinegar.
UCCE uses heat-treated or pasteurized whey, pasteurized whole milk and vinegar of 5% acidity.
For 1 gallon of whey, the UCCE table gives 12.8 oz of milk and 1.3 oz (2 tablespoons + 2 teaspoons) of vinegar.
For 1 quart of whey, it gives 3.2 oz of milk and 0.32 oz (2 teaspoons) of vinegar.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): use whey only from cheese made with pasteurized milk.
Add the whole milk to the fresh whey and heat it to 185 °F (85 °C); small curd particles will form.
Add about 2 teaspoons of vinegar per quart of whey slowly, stirring gently, and more if needed, until the whey is quite clear.
Adding the vinegar slowly over about 5 minutes gives a better curd.
Pour everything into a cloth to separate the curd; once it has drained, the ricotta is ready to eat.
The whey ricotta recipe gives no storage time.
For its whole-milk ricotta, UCCE says it keeps in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to a week, or in the freezer for up to 6 months.
NMSU, on which this recipe is based, says soft cheese keeps only 5–7 days in the refrigerator.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): keep whey ricotta in an airtight container in the refrigerator and eat it within 5 days.
Pregnant women should avoid cheeses made from unpasteurized milk.
